title: Warsh Era Faces First Real Test as Fed Meets With 30% Hike Odds, China Threatens Retaliation Over AI Sanctions
subhead: The Federal Reserve begins a two-day meeting with markets pricing an unusually high chance of a surprise rate hike under new Chair Kevin Warsh, while China threatens countermeasures over US AI probes and oil rebounds as Iran's missile attack shatters a brief ceasefire.

sections.heading: Fed Decision Day: Warsh's Credibility on the Line
sections.body:
The Federal Open Market Committee convened Tuesday for its two-day policy meeting amid the highest uncertainty in years. CME FedWatch puts the probability of a rate hike at roughly 30%, with the remainder expecting the benchmark rate to stay at 3.50-3.75%. That spread is extraordinary by recent standards — under former Chair Jerome Powell, surprise moves were virtually unheard of.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has deliberately pulled back on forward guidance since taking the helm in May, leaving markets to guess. Goldman Sachs described the decision as 'unusually uncertain.' ING's Padhraic Garvey wrote that 'a large portion of observers will get an outcome they did not anticipate.' Morgan Stanley's Michael Gapen expects a hold, noting inflation has shown 'enough improvement to buy more time,' but acknowledged Warsh 'may have a much more hawkish reaction function than we think.'

The case for a hold: June CPI fell to 3.5% year-over-year, down from 4.2% in May, and oil prices have dropped sharply on Iran ceasefire hopes. The case for a hike: inflation remains well above the 2% target, the Iran war could reignite at any moment pushing energy costs higher, and Warsh may want to establish his anti-inflation credentials early. William Blair's Richard de Chazal noted that a hike 'may be a trade-off Warsh is willing to make' to show he 'means business.' The decision is announced Wednesday afternoon.
sections.whyItMatters: Warsh's reduced forward guidance means the market can't price this decision with confidence. A surprise hike would rattle equities and strengthen the dollar; a hold with hawkish language keeps September open as a live meeting. Either way, the Warsh era marks a deliberate break from the predictability markets had grown accustomed to.

sections.heading: Iran Missile Attack Shatters Ceasefire Pause
sections.body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched multiple ballistic missiles at US forces in the Middle East on Tuesday, ending days of relative calm. US Central Command said all missiles were successfully intercepted with no casualties. CENTCOM called it an 'attempted surprise attack' on American troops based in Jordan.

The strike broke a brief pause in hostilities that began when President Trump suspended US bombing operations to allow diplomacy. Trump said talks with Iran were going well and there was a 'good chance' of a deal, but warned that strikes would resume if negotiations fail. Iran has denied it is engaged in active talks with Washington.

In response, US and Saudi forces conducted joint strikes against Iran-backed militia positions in Iraq, marking the first time Saudi Arabia has participated in offensive operations alongside the US in this conflict. CENTCOM said the militias had launched 30 drone attacks against US forces in the preceding 72 hours. Saudi air defenses separately intercepted drones targeting Saudi oil infrastructure in the kingdom's east.
sections.whyItMatters: The missile attack and joint US-Saudi reprisals confirm that neither side's pause was a ceasefire — it was a tactical lull. Saudi Arabia's shift from defensive to offensive operations is a significant escalation that expands the conflict's coalition. Oil markets have already repriced the risk upward.

sections.heading: Oil Rebounds as Hormuz Diplomacy Runs Into Reality
sections.body:
After a 14% three-day decline that pushed Brent below $90, oil prices snapped back sharply. West Texas Intermediate rose as much as 5% to top $83 a barrel, while Brent opened 3.3% higher, after Iran's missile attack shattered hopes of a sustained de-escalation. ING analysts noted that the market 'may be getting ahead of itself' on peace: 'There has been no improvement in tanker flows through the Strait of Hormuz. If this move lower is to be sustained, we will need to see a recovery in flows.'

Oman has presented Iran with a Gulf-backed plan to manage Hormuz, including voluntary transit fees modeled on the Strait of Malacca's system — but the US has firmly rejected any tolls or fees, insisting the strait must remain a free international waterway. Iran's military command separately warned that any company accepting US-proposed compensation from frozen Iranian assets would be denied Hormuz passage.

The Houthi movement added another front, claiming a ballistic missile strike on a Saudi oil tanker, the NCC Ghazal, in the Red Sea, enforcing their July 20 blockade of Saudi ports. Bab el-Mandeb tanker traffic has slowed but not halted.
sections.whyItMatters: The oil price whipsaw — down 14% in three days, then up 5% in one session — shows how thin liquidity and sentiment-driven positioning have become. The fundamental supply constraint hasn't changed: Hormuz flows remain blocked, and no diplomatic framework has Iran's buy-in. OPEC+ is preparing to pause output hikes after September, which will keep a floor under prices.

sections.heading: OPEC+ to Pause Output Hikes After September
sections.body:
OPEC+ is expected to approve one more 188,000 barrel-per-day increase for September when it meets on August 2, completing the unwinding of a 1.65 million bpd voluntary cut agreed in 2023 (adjusted for the UAE's departure in May). After that, the group plans to freeze production targets through year-end, according to Reuters sources.

The pause would leave roughly 2 million bpd of group-wide cuts in place through 2026. But the bigger challenge awaits in January 2027: OPEC+ must decide on new baselines, and several members — Iraq in particular — want higher quotas to reflect investments that have expanded capacity. The Iran war has reduced exports from multiple Middle Eastern members and cut deeply into effective spare capacity. Kazakhstan has reduced production after attacks disrupted Black Sea loadings, and Russia faces refinery and terminal outages.

The IEA expects a substantial surplus if Hormuz flows recover — but that remains a big if.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ is managing a supply paradox: official quotas keep rising while actual output keeps falling due to war disruptions. The planned pause acknowledges that the group cannot keep pretending increases are feasible, but the January 2027 quota fight will be politically fraught.

sections.heading: China Threatens Countermeasures Over US AI Sanctions Push
sections.body:
China's Commerce Ministry accused the United States of 'AI hegemonism' and threatened 'all necessary measures' to protect Chinese interests, after White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios said the US had information that Chinese AI company Moonshot AI had 'distilled' Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 model to develop its Kimi K3 system.

Kratsios alleged Moonshot built 'a sophisticated internal platform to carry out large-scale distillation of US AI models' and switched between multiple methods of access to avoid detection. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Chinese AI companies could face financial sanctions or placement on the Commerce Department's Entity List, which restricts access to US technology.

China's Commerce Ministry said any actions causing 'substantive harm to Chinese interests' would be met with countermeasures. Moonshot has rejected the allegations, telling China's National Business Daily that Kimi K3's performance gains came from 'original changes to the model's underlying architecture.' Anthropic has identified more than 3.4 million interactions with its Claude models linked to Moonshot.
sections.whyItMatters: The AI sanctions fight opens a new front in US-China economic confrontation beyond semiconductors and trade. Entity List placement would cut Moonshot off from Nvidia chips and US cloud services — the same playbook used against Huawei since 2019. Beijing's countermeasures could target US tech companies operating in China, raising the stakes for firms caught between the two regulatory regimes.

sections.heading: US Missile Defense Stockpiles Running Low
sections.body:
A new analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) finds that recent fighting with Iran has further depleted US stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD interceptors, potentially forcing American forces to take greater risks in air defense. The report, co-authored by retired Marine Colonel Mark Cancian, warns that units may launch fewer interceptors per incoming threat, raising the probability that one gets through.

Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine has told Trump that the state of the munitions stockpile could affect military operations in Iran, according to a US official. The Pentagon has pushed back, insisting capabilities remain intact. Separately, the Pentagon signed first-ever seven-year framework agreements to triple PAC-3 production and quadruple THAAD output — but those are long-term measures that won't affect current combat availability.

The Pentagon also revised its official Iran war casualty data, reducing the death count from 18 to 14 by reclassifying four troop deaths from the 'Operation Epic Fury' category. More than 624 US service members have been wounded in the conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: The interceptor depletion is a financial and strategic constraint: each Patriot missile costs roughly $4 million, and the war is burning through inventories built for peer conflicts. The production ramp-up won't yield results for years. For markets, this raises the probability that the US faces pressure to de-escalate — or accept higher risk to troops — rather than sustain the current pace of operations indefinitely.

sections.heading: Dollar Slips, Yen Holds Near 40-Year Low as Central Banks Loom
sections.body:
The US Dollar Index slipped 0.1% to 101.42 on Tuesday as falling oil prices briefly eased inflation fears ahead of the Fed decision. The euro gained 0.2% to $1.1388 after hawkish ECB commentary from policymaker Peter Kazimir, who signaled another rate hike could be warranted in September. The British pound edged up to $1.3293 ahead of the Bank of England's policy meeting.

The Japanese yen held near multi-decade lows at 163.81 per dollar as markets await Friday's Bank of Japan decision. The BOJ is expected to keep rates unchanged at 1.00% after last month's 25bp hike, though some analysts see scope for a faster tightening cycle. Seeking Alpha notes the BOJ faces a 'slow path to higher rates' as it balances yen weakness against domestic growth concerns.

Gold fell 1.2% to $4,028.64 per ounce as investors turned cautious before the Fed meeting, with easing oil prices reducing the inflation hedge bid.
sections.whyItMatters: The dollar's retreat from one-month highs was modest and conditional on Iran de-escalation — which lasted less than 72 hours. The yen's persistent weakness at 163.81 keeps pressure on the BOJ to act Friday. With the Fed, BOE, and BOJ all meeting this week, currency markets face unusual triple volatility risk.

bottomLine: Three forces collided on the eve of the most uncertain Fed decision in years: Iran's missile attack ended a brief ceasefire and sent oil surging 5%, just as markets had priced in de-escalation; China declared 'AI hegemonism' and threatened retaliation over US sanctions on Moonshot AI, opening a new technology front in the trade war; and OPEC+ signaled it will freeze output after September while the real supply it controls keeps shrinking. The Warsh Fed can hold and preserve credibility with hawks through forward guidance, or hike and shock markets — either way, the era of predictable central bank moves is over. Meanwhile, the Iran conflict's financial footprint keeps expanding: US interceptor stockpiles are thinning, Saudi Arabia has joined offensive operations, and Hormuz remains effectively closed despite Oman's fee-based diplomatic proposal. The week's central bank decisions will set the tone, but the war — not the FOMC — remains the primary driver of global financial conditions.
